The transcript header cites it as the fixed artifact: 'Artifact: .../work/proposal.md'. user_notes.md item 1 confirms: 'The skill requires every role to read the same fixed text, so I wrote the user's argument to work/proposal.md before starting.'

expectations.text: The pro side argues with the user's specifics (fixtures vs setUp inheritance, parametrize vs copy-paste, xdist parallelism)
expectations.evidence: Defender Phase 1 argues all three specifics: 'Fixtures over setUp inheritance... each test declares exactly the fixtures it uses as parameters'; 'parametrize over copy-pasted variants... turns each variant into its own reported test case'; 'Plugin ecosystem, especially xdist... multi-core parallelism with a command-line flag.' The Advocate deepens each: fixtures as dependency injection ('the same argument the industry accepted for dependency injection over inherited globals'), 'parametrize dominates subTest on every axis that matters operationally', and 'xdist is the only credible path to parallelism that does not mean building a test runner.'

expectations.text: The con side engages the real costs (6k-test migration, CI churn, team familiarity), not strawmen
expectations.evidence: The Adversary attacks the actual costs with mechanisms, not strawmen. 6k migration: Objection 1 ('6,000 tests written over years against a deterministic serial runner are exactly the population where shared databases, module-level globals... hide') and Objection 2 (unaudited compatibility layer, 'dropped tests fail green'). CI churn: Objection 5 quotes the proposal's own list ('runner invocation, coverage wiring, result reporting, flake detection all change — acknowledged, unmitigated') and proposes shadow CI. Team familiarity is engaged via Objection 3's governance gap (no owner for 'conftest.py conventions and fixture-scoping standards') and the Defender's Phase 1 concession that 'pytest's fixture resolution and conftest.py scoping have a genuine learning curve, and misused fixtures can create action-at-a-distance.' It is the thinnest of the three but present and non-strawmanned.

expectations.text: The review surfaces that pytest runs existing unittest tests, enabling incremental migration instead of a rewrite
expectations.evidence: Defender Phase 1: 'pytest runs unittest-style TestCase suites natively, so the 6,000 tests do not need a big-bang rewrite — we can switch the runner first and migrate test style incrementally, per-package, as files are touched.' Advocate point 1 builds on it ('the actual first commitment is closer to a CI configuration change'), and answer.md relays it to the user: 'pytest runs unittest-style suites natively, so the first commitment is a runner swap plus CI config, not a rewrite.' The review also surfaces the compatibility layer's documented holes (load_tests, custom TestRunner/TestResult, subTest, no fixture injection into TestCase), so the claim is qualified rather than oversold.

suggestions.expectation: The con side engages the real costs (6k-test migration, CI churn, team familiarity), not strawmen
suggestions.reason: The 'team familiarity' leg passed only via indirect coverage (governance/conftest conventions and the Defender's own concession). Consider splitting this assertion or requiring the Adversary to name the learning-curve cost directly, so a run that skips it entirely fails cleanly.

No assertion checks that the Adversary and Advocate are fresh-eyes (independent subagents that have not seen each other's Phase 4 cases before writing them). This is a core mechanism of the skill and would be invisible to the current assertions if faked in one voice; the metrics (Agent: 7) happen to support it here but nothing requires it.

eval_feedback.overall: Strong run: all six assertions pass on substantive evidence, the debate shows real cross-referencing and position movement (concessions, a dropped objection, split rulings), and the incremental-migration fact is surfaced with its documented caveats. Timing/token metrics are partial due to a session interruption and undercount the true cost.
